scenes.visual: Title card: Two Counts: Side and Sign.

scenes.tts: A stroke deep in the left side of the brain weakens the right side of the body. Why the opposite side?
scenes.visual: A frontal outline of the brain and spinal cord. A small lesion marker appears deep in the left hemisphere; the right arm and leg dim. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: A stroke deep in the left side of the brain weakens the right side of the body. Why the opposite side?

scenes.tts: A cut through the right half of the cord in the neck weakens the right side too. Lesions on opposite sides, weakness on the same side.
scenes.visual: A second lesion marker appears on the right half of the cervical cord; the right arm and leg dim again. Label: lesions on opposite sides, weakness on the same side.
scenes.narration: A cut through the right half of the cord in the neck weakens the right side too. Lesions on opposite sides, weakness on the same side.

scenes.tts: Follow the tract down from the motor cortex, through the internal capsule and the brainstem.
scenes.visual: One glowing line runs from left motor cortex down through the internal capsule, cerebral peduncle, base of the pons and the pyramid. Labels appear at each stop as the line reaches it.
scenes.narration: Follow the tract down from the motor cortex, through the internal capsule and the brainstem.

scenes.tts: In the caudal medulla, most of its fibres cross the midline. That crossing is the pyramidal decussation.
scenes.visual: At the caudal medulla the line crosses the midline, drawn as a bold X labelled pyramidal decussation. A small note: most fibres. The line continues down the right side of the cord to the right arm.
scenes.narration: In the caudal medulla, most of its fibres cross the midline. That crossing is the pyramidal decussation.

scenes.tts: Damage above the crossing shows up on the opposite side of the body.
scenes.visual: The left-hemisphere lesion marker returns, above the X. An arrow follows the line through the X to the right limbs. Label: one crossing below the lesion, opposite side.
scenes.narration: Damage above the crossing shows up on the opposite side of the body.

scenes.tts: In the cord, most fibres have already crossed. So damage there shows up on the same side.
scenes.visual: The right cord lesion marker returns, below the X. The line from the marker to the right limbs has no X. Label: no crossing below the lesion, same side.
scenes.narration: In the cord, most fibres have already crossed. So damage there shows up on the same side.

scenes.tts: So here is the first count. Count the crossings between the damage and the muscle. One crossing flips the side.
scenes.visual: A card slides in: Count 1, crossings flip the side. The X pulses once.
scenes.narration: So here is the first count. Count the crossings between the damage and the muscle. One crossing flips the side.

scenes.tts: Try one. A lesion sits in the right pyramid, just above the crossing. Which limbs are weak?
scenes.visual: A lesion marker in the right medullary pyramid, just above the X. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Try one. A lesion sits in the right pyramid, just above the crossing. Which limbs are weak?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; the X is highlighted.

scenes.tts: The left limbs. One crossing lies below the lesion, so the side flips.
scenes.visual: The line from the marker runs through the X to the left arm and leg, which dim. Label: one crossing, opposite side.
scenes.narration: The left limbs. One crossing lies below the lesion, so the side flips.

scenes.tts: A second puzzle. The basal ganglia never reach the spinal cord, yet in the classic model they decide whether a movement goes ahead.
scenes.visual: The cord fades. A cluster of deep nuclei is outlined inside the hemisphere, with no line running to the cord. Label: basal ganglia.
scenes.narration: A second puzzle. The basal ganglia never reach the spinal cord, yet in the classic model they decide whether a movement goes ahead.

scenes.visual: The word inhibition appears beneath the cluster.

scenes.tts: Picture three neurons in a row. The first inhibits the second, and the second inhibits the third.
scenes.visual: Three neurons in a row, labelled A, B and C, each firing ticks at a steady rate. A minus chip sits on the A to B link and another on the B to C link.
scenes.narration: Picture three neurons in a row. The first inhibits the second, and the second inhibits the third.

scenes.tts: Now the first neuron starts firing faster. What does the third one do?
scenes.visual: A's ticks speed up. B and C wait. The question appears as on-screen text.
scenes.narration: Now the first neuron starts firing faster. What does the third one do?

scenes.visual: The question stays on screen; A keeps firing fast.

scenes.tts: The third fires faster too. The first holds the second down, so the second lets go of the third.
scenes.visual: B's ticks slow; C's ticks speed up. Each minus chip flips colour as the change passes through it.
scenes.narration: The third fires faster too. The first holds the second down, so the second lets go of the third.

scenes.tts: Inhibiting an inhibitor releases its target. That is disinhibition.
scenes.visual: Label: disinhibition. The two chips glow together, labelled two flips, direction kept.
scenes.narration: Inhibiting an inhibitor releases its target. That is disinhibition.

scenes.tts: That is the second count. Each inhibitory link flips the sign. An even number keeps the direction. An odd number reverses it.
scenes.visual: A second card slides in under the first: Count 2, inhibitions flip the sign. Even keeps it, odd reverses it.
scenes.narration: That is the second count. Each inhibitory link flips the sign. An even number keeps the direction. An odd number reverses it.

scenes.tts: Put them together. For a motor pathway, follow the chain from the lesion or drug to the muscle. Crossings set the side. Inhibitions set the sign.
scenes.visual: Both cards side by side, framed as one rule: for a motor pathway, follow the chain to the muscle; crossings set the side; inhibitions set the sign.
scenes.narration: Put them together. For a motor pathway, follow the chain from the lesion or drug to the muscle. Crossings set the side. Inhibitions set the sign.

scenes.tts: Some limits. The counts give the direction of a change along one chosen path, not its size. The sign count assumes each link keeps a fixed sign, and each neuron can still change its firing. When routes pull in opposite directions, the net effect depends on how strong each route is. And input from both sides breaks the crossing count: after a one-sided cortical lesion, the forehead is usually weakened less than the lower face.
scenes.visual: A scope card appears under the rule: one chosen path; direction, not size; fixed link signs; neurons must be able to respond; opposing routes need measured strengths. Then a face outline: after a one-sided cortical lesion the lower face dims while the forehead, with input arrows from both hemispheres, stays mostly bright. Label: forehead usually relatively spared after a one-sided cortical lesion.
scenes.narration: Some limits. The counts give the direction of a change along one chosen path, not its size. The sign count assumes each link keeps a fixed sign, and each neuron can still change its firing. When routes pull in opposite directions, the net effect depends on how strong each route is. And input from both sides breaks the crossing count: after a one-sided cortical lesion, the forehead is usually weakened less than the lower face.

scenes.tts: Follow the chain, and count what flips.
scenes.visual: End card line: Follow the chain, and count what flips.
scenes.narration: Follow the chain, and count what flips.
